meta.blurb: One quiet summer night, a shooting star falls on a common outside London. Soon giant machines are marching across England, burning everything in their path. A writer survives the invasion from Mars, and learns what really saved the Earth.
meta.bible: Narrator: a writer who lives in Woking, an ordinary man, thoughtful and honest, never named. Wife: the narrator's wife, whom he sends to Leatherhead. Ogilvy: an astronomer at Ottershaw who first sees the Martians. Henderson: a London journalist at the first pit. Stent: the Astronomer Royal. Martians: creatures from Mars, large heads, huge dark eyes, tentacles, a V-shaped mouth, clever and cold. Mars: the red planet, older than Earth and dying. Cylinders: the ten metal capsules that fall from Mars. Heat-Ray: the invisible beam that burns whatever it touches. Tripods: the three-legged fighting machines, taller than houses. Black Smoke: a poison cloud that the Martians fire in shells. Red Weed: the strange red plant that spreads from the pits. Horsell Common: the sandy common near Woking where the first cylinder lands. Woking: the narrator's town in Surrey. Surrey: the county south of London. Chobham: a village near Woking. Weybridge: a town on the River Thames. Shepperton: a town on the Thames. Thames: the river. Leatherhead: where the narrator's wife stays. Sheen: where the narrator hides in a ruined house. Putney Hill: where the narrator meets the Artilleryman. Primrose Hill: where the narrator finds the last Martians. London: the great city. Curate: a weak, frightened clergyman who hides with the narrator. Artilleryman: a soldier with big dreams of living underground. Brother: the narrator's brother, a medical student in London. Mrs Elphinstone: a lady whom the brother helps. Miss Elphinstone: her young sister-in-law. Thunder Child: a brave ironclad ship of the Royal Navy. Ulla: the Martians' cry. Bacteria: the tiny germs that kill the Martians. Voice and tone: calm, serious and vivid, told after the event by one who survived; the horror is real but never gory; the end brings quiet relief and thoughtfulness.

A1A2: Long ago, people on Earth were calm, but minds on Mars were watching them.
Ogilvy saw a bright flash on Mars, but most people did not care.
One night, a shooting star fell onto Horsell Common near the narrator's town.
In the morning, a huge metal cylinder lay in a deep sand pit.
A crowd stood around the pit, and the top of the cylinder began to turn.
The top fell off, and a strange gray creature with big eyes came out.
Brave men walked toward the pit with a white flag, but a flash killed them.
The narrator ran through the dark and hid, very afraid.
At home, he saw soldiers on the common, but nobody understood the danger.
That night, he drove his wife to Leatherhead to keep her safe.
On the way back, a huge machine with three legs walked through the storm.
At home, he watched the soldiers fight the Martian machines.
He met a tired soldier, and they decided to leave the burning town.
In Weybridge, soldiers fired their guns at the Martians, and one machine fell.
The Martians made the river boil, and the narrator escaped with a curate.
The two men walked through smoke and ruined fields, and the curate lost hope.
In London, the narrator's brother read about the Martians in a newspaper.
Soon people were afraid, and the brother left London with thousands of others.
On the road, he helped two ladies, and they traveled together.
At the coast, they got on a crowded boat and sailed away.
A brave ship of war, the Thunder Child, fought the Martians and saved the boats.
The narrator and the curate hid in a ruined house when another cylinder fell.
Through a small hole in the wall, he watched the Martians in the pit.
The Martians made new machines and used fresh blood as their food.
The two men stayed in the house for many days, hungry and afraid.
The curate lost his mind and shouted, and the narrator was very afraid.
A Martian took the curate away, and the narrator hid in the dark.
After many days, everything was quiet, and the pit seemed to be empty.
Outside, a strange red weed from Mars was growing everywhere.
He walked toward London and met the soldier again on Putney Hill.
The soldier had a big dream about building a new city under the ground.
The narrator saw that it was only a dream, and he walked away.
London was empty and silent, and he heard a sad cry: “Ulla, ulla!”
He felt too tired to hide, so he walked toward the cry.
There he found a still machine, and a dead Martian lay beside it.
More dead Martians lay across the city, and birds were eating them.
Tiny germs on Earth had killed the Martians, and no army could do that.
The narrator cried, and slowly the people of London came out again.
A kind family looked after him, and he heard news from other countries.
Everywhere people heard the good news, and the trains started to run again.
He walked home to Woking, and his house was silent and empty.
Then he heard a voice, and he saw his wife, alive.
They held each other, and he thanked God for her.
The Martian machines were put in museums, and scientists studied them.
People learned that Earth is small and not the only place with life.
The narrator looked at Mars, small and red, and he wondered about the future.
People were different now, and they were kinder and more careful.
He lived a quiet life, but sometimes he dreamed about the black machines.
Now he looks at the sun and the world with new eyes.
He is thankful for every quiet evening, and his story ends in peace.
B1B2: In the last years of the nineteenth century, people believed that nothing could disturb the peace of their small world. Yet across space, minds far older and colder than ours were studying the Earth and making their plans.
One night, the astronomer Ogilvy sees a bright flash of gas burst from the surface of Mars. Few people take any notice, although the flashes come again, once every night, for ten nights.

Then, one night, a shooting star falls from the sky and lands with a heavy thud on Horsell Common, near Woking. The narrator, who has seen it burning across the dark, goes out to find it the next morning.

At dawn, he finds a huge pit with a smoking metal cylinder lying at the bottom, and it is far too hot to touch. Ogilvy and the journalist Henderson are standing at the edge, and they look at it with growing wonder.

All day, more and more people arrive from Woking to stare at the cylinder, and some of them poke it with sticks. Then, a dull scraping sound comes from inside, and the top of the cylinder begins to turn slowly.

At last, the lid falls off and rolls into the sand, and the crowd pushes back in terror. A gray, wet, shapeless creature with huge dark eyes and a V-shaped mouth drags itself slowly up into the light.
A small group of men, led by Ogilvy and a man called Stent, walks toward the pit carrying a white flag. Without any warning, a beam of fire leaps out and the Heat-Ray burns them all to ashes.
The narrator, who is standing at the edge of the common, turns and runs as fast as he can through the dark. Not until he reaches a ditch far away does he stop, shaking and gasping for breath.

At home, he finds the evening just as it was, and he wonders whether the whole thing could have been a dream. Soon, soldiers arrive and surround the common, but nobody in Woking knows how great the danger is.

On Friday night, the narrator sees the night sky light up as more cylinders fall from the heavens. He decides that his wife must go, so he drives her in a hired cart to stay with relatives in Leatherhead.
On the way home, a terrible thunderstorm breaks, and flashes of lightning light up the country. In one of them, he sees a gigantic machine on three legs walk across the fields, taller than a house.
The narrator reaches his house and watches from an upstairs window as the soldiers fire at the machines. The Martians answer with the Heat-Ray, and in a minute whole rows of houses burst into flames.
In the garden, he meets a tired soldier, an artilleryman, who has escaped from the battle. They agree that nothing can stop the Martians, and that they must run if they want to stay alive.
At Weybridge, the army fires at the Martians, and one of the machines falls into the river. The others strike back with their Heat-Rays and a deadly cloud of Black Smoke that creeps along the ground.

The narrator and a nervous curate find a boat on the Thames and push out into the river. The Martians sweep the water with their Heat-Rays, and the river boils with steam, but the two men escape alive.
The two men walk across a burned and silent countryside, looking for a place to hide. The curate, who has lost his hope, cries out that it is the end of the world, and the narrator cannot calm him.

Meanwhile, the narrator's brother, a medical student, reads about the Martians in a London newspaper. He is puzzled, because the news seems too strange to be true, and most of the people around him do not believe it.
Soon the news gets worse, and London is filled with fear, and people crowd the trains and the roads. The brother leaves the city with thousands of others, walking through the dust under the hot sun.
On the road, he sees two men attack a little carriage with two ladies in it. The brother beats them off, and the grateful ladies ask him to travel with them toward the sea.
At the coast, they find a crowded steamer ready to sail and pay the captain for a place on it. Behind them, a great crowd of frightened people stands on the shore, waiting for the next boat.

Suddenly, two Martian machines stride toward the boats, but a warship called the Thunder Child steams boldly out to meet them. It destroys both machines before it is hit, and the steamers sail safely away into the mist.
The narrator and the curate hide in a ruined house at Sheen, where they cannot be seen. In the night, a great cylinder crashes down beside it, and the house falls half to pieces around their heads.
Next morning, the narrator creeps to a crack in the broken wall and looks down into the new pit. What he sees there is something that no one has ever seen before, and it fills him with horror.

The Martians are working on huge shining machines, and he sees that they are almost all head and hands. He also sees that they feed on the fresh blood of living creatures, and he shrinks from the crack.
For days, the two men are prisoners in the ruined house and must be quiet if they want to survive. They have almost nothing to eat or drink, and they listen to every sound from the pit.
As time passes, the curate becomes wild and hungry and begins to talk and shout in his fear. The narrator, who knows that the Martians might hear him, tries again and again to quiet him.
At last the curate's voice becomes so loud that one of the Martians sends a long arm into the house to find him. The narrator hides in the dark, and the creature carries the curate away.
For many days, the narrator stays hidden in the cellar, hardly daring to breathe. Then, one morning, he hears no sound at all from the pit, and he wonders if the Martians are gone.

He climbs out and finds that the whole pit is empty, and that red weed is spreading everywhere across the land. The strange plant has covered the ruins and has even choked the rivers, and he stares at it in wonder.
He decides to walk toward London, because he does not know where else to go. On Putney Hill, he meets the artilleryman again, who greets him like an old friend.

The artilleryman says that men are finished above ground, and that those who live must make a new world beneath the streets. He talks of tunnels, machines and a fresh start, and his eyes shine with excitement.
But as the day goes on, the narrator sees that this man will only ever talk, and that he will never dig a single stone. He says goodbye, shakes the soldier's hand and walks on toward the city.
London is empty and silent, and the great houses stand with their windows broken and their doors open. Suddenly he hears a strange, sad wailing sound coming from far away: “Ulla, ulla, ulla.”
He is so tired and lonely that he no longer cares what happens to him, and he walks toward the sound. He crosses a wide field to Primrose Hill, where he expects to meet the Martians.
Instead, he finds a Martian machine standing perfectly still, with its great body bent over. A dead Martian lies in it, and the dogs and crows are already eating its remains.
All over London the narrator finds dead Martians, still in their machines or lying beside them. Slowly he understands that the invasion has ended, and the sad cry is the last Martian call.

The Martians have died from the tiny germs that live in our air and water, which no army could ever fight. We carry these germs in us, and our bodies are used to them, but the Martians had no defense.
The narrator weeps with relief, and the people of London come cautiously out of their houses and look at the sky. Day by day, the great city wakes up from its nightmare and begins to live again.
The narrator is weak and ill from hunger, but a kind family finds him and takes him in. They nurse him back to health, and little by little, he hears what has happened in the rest of the world.

Everywhere, in towns and cities, people heard that the Martians were dead, and a great wave of joy and thanks spread across the planet. Trains began to run again, shops opened, and families came home.
At last the narrator is strong enough to travel, and he takes a train toward Woking and goes to his own home. He finds the door closed and the house silent, with a layer of dust over everything.
As he stands in the doorway, he hears a quiet footstep and a voice that he knows. He turns around and sees his wife standing there, whom he had feared he had lost for ever.
They hold each other tightly and say nothing for a long time, and he thanks God for her return. For him, this is the greatest joy of all, and he knows how lucky he is.
The Martian machines are carried away, and scientists study them with great care in the museums of the world. The men of science learn a good deal about the minds and the bodies of the Martians.
People begin to see that the Earth is a small world among many, and that mankind is not alone. They learn that life may come from other places, and that nothing in the universe is certain.
On clear nights, the narrator looks up at Mars glowing small and red in the sky and wonders. Perhaps the Martians will come again, or perhaps men will one day build their own ships and visit Mars.
Men and women seem different now, as if the war has made them gentler and more careful of one another. They have learned that their peace can be broken in a day, and they treasure each hour of it.
The narrator lives a quiet life now, but he often dreams of the Martian machines and wakes up afraid. Then he sees his wife asleep beside him, and he feels the cold fear slowly fade.

Now he looks at the world around him differently, because he has seen how easily everything could be lost. The sun on the road and the green fields have become dear to him, and he sees them with new eyes.
He ends his book with a feeling of thanks for the ordinary world and all of its small, daily kindnesses. In the quiet of the evening, he sits with his family and looks up at the first star.
C1C2: Toward the end of the nineteenth century, hardly anyone imagined that our world was being studied, patiently and with great interest, by minds far more advanced than any on Earth, though just as mortal. Across the dark gulf of space, those minds, cold and without pity, looked at our green planet with hungry eyes, and slowly, step by step, they prepared to take it. Meanwhile, people went about their small daily business, comfortable in the belief that nothing could ever challenge their rule.

On one clear evening, the astronomer Ogilvy, peering through the eyepiece of his telescope at the planet Mars, saw a jet of glowing gas burst from its red surface. Few people paid any attention, for the world was busy with its own concerns, and those who did noticed only a faint and distant flicker. Yet the flashes returned night after night, and not one of them could be explained by any natural cause that the learned men of that age knew.

On the tenth night after the first flash, a shooting star streaked across the heavens, trailing a green fire, and struck the ground with a dull thud on Horsell Common, not far from Woking. The narrator, who had watched it fall from the window of his study, walked out in the first light of morning to find where it had landed. He did not know that he was going to look upon the first stroke of the greatest struggle that humanity had ever faced.

At the edge of a deep pit in the sand, with the earth torn open around it and the heather scorched, lay an enormous cylinder, half buried and so hot that no one could touch it. Ogilvy and the journalist Henderson stood beside it, and, in their astonishment, they spoke in low voices, as if the thing might hear. It was clearly not a meteorite, since its surface was smooth and was scored with strange patterns, and an odd sound of scraping seemed to come from within it.

All through the day, more and more people trickled out from Woking to stare at the strange object, and children came to throw stones at it and run away laughing. A little before sunset, the dull scraping sound began again, and with a slow and steady screwing noise, the top of the cylinder began to turn. The crowd, who had been so noisy, fell quiet, and a man cried out that there must be someone inside who needed help.

At last, with a ringing crash, the lid fell and rolled down the slope of the pit, and the people at the edge staggered back in horror at what they saw. Out of the dark mouth of the cylinder rose a grey, glistening shape, as large as a bear, with enormous dark eyes, a V-shaped mouth that dripped with moisture, and a cluster of writhing tentacles. It struggled slowly to the edge, heavy and clumsy under the drag of the Earth, and fell back with a wet, groaning cry.

Soon afterward, a small party of brave men, among them Ogilvy and the astronomer Stent, advanced down the slope toward the pit, waving a white flag in the hope of speaking with the creatures. Suddenly, a little glow of green light shone out of the pit, and a bright beam of heat swung across the sand and touched the bushes, the men and the trees, bursting everything into flame. The Heat-Ray had come, and in a single moment, every one of the messengers was dead.

The narrator, who had been standing among the crowd at the edge of the common, turned and ran blindly through the darkness, falling over roots and sliding down banks as the flames spread behind him. His heart pounded as though it would burst, and he could not stop to think, for the one thought in his mind was that he must get as far away as he could. At last, trembling in the shelter of a ditch, he crouched and waited for the terror to pass.

When at last he reached home, the narrator found the lamps lit and the supper table laid, and for a moment he wondered whether it had all been a nightmare. Out beyond the end of the road, the heather was burning, and soldiers began to arrive and form lines around the sand pits, quite sure that a few well-aimed shots would soon end the matter. Nobody in Woking could yet imagine that these creatures were far more terrible than any enemy an army had ever met.

That night, the narrator saw more green stars falling out of the sky, one after another, and he knew with a sudden chill that the Martians were not alone and that more were on their way. He resolved to take his wife to safety at once, so he borrowed a horse and cart, and he drove her through the dark to her cousins' house at Leatherhead. They said very little on the road, for both of them were afraid of what lay ahead.

On his return journey, a violent thunderstorm broke over the dark countryside, and the lightning cut the black sky into jagged pieces. In one of those dazzling flashes, the narrator saw something that stopped his breath: a gigantic machine, taller than any house, moving on three jointed legs and striding across the fields like a vast and metallic man. It was gone as the darkness closed in, but the memory of it stayed with him for the rest of his life.

By the time he reached his house, the storm had passed, and from an upstairs window he could see the night alive with flashes and flames, where the soldiers were fighting the machines on the plain below. The Martians answered with their Heat-Ray, sweeping it across the country like a gigantic scythe, and in a few minutes whole streets of houses burst into fire. He watched, powerless and horrified, as the army that was to save England was swept aside like a heap of dry leaves.

At dawn, in the ruins of his garden, the narrator was startled by a figure in the half-light, a tired and dusty soldier of the artillery who had escaped from the battle. The two men spoke briefly and bitterly of what they had seen, and agreed that no gun, no army and no courage could prevail against creatures of such power. Within an hour, they had parted, each of them setting out through the smoke in search of some place that was still safe.

At Weybridge, the army turned out in force, and as the narrator watched from a distance, the guns thundered along the bank of the Thames and brought down one of the machines with a mighty crash. The others, however, struck back at once with a cloud of poisonous Black Smoke that crept along the ground, and with the Heat-Ray, whose invisible beam turned steam and flame upon the soldiers. The narrator saw the defense crumble, and he knew that he was witnessing the first great defeat of mankind.

With a frightened curate whom he had met among the ruins, the narrator found a boat and pushed out into the middle of the Thames, hoping that the river might carry them away. The Martians swept the water with their Heat-Rays, and the river bubbled and boiled with scalding steam, while the two men lay down in the bottom of the boat and prayed. Somehow they escaped the blast and crept ashore, scalded and exhausted but still alive.

The two men crossed a blackened, silent country, where trees had been reduced to charcoal and the grass was scorched to the roots, and the whole land seemed to be dead. The curate, who had been a timid man even in his own parish, began to weep and to cry aloud that this was the end of the world and the judgment of heaven. The narrator, who had lost patience with this display, found that he had no words left with which to answer him.

Meanwhile, in London, the narrator's brother, a medical student, picked up his morning paper and read of a strange happening in Surrey, where a mysterious cylinder had fallen out of the sky. The account was short, vague and strangely calm, and at first the people around him, who were hurrying to work, laughed at it as one more of the wild stories that fill the papers. He felt, though, a growing sense of dread that would not leave him, however hard he tried to read the rest of the page and then to put the matter out of his mind.

Day by day, the news grew worse, and by Sunday the whole of London had begun to understand that something terrible was approaching from the south and west. Crowds filled the stations, and in the streets the roads were jammed with carts and wagons, so the brother, who had no wish to wait for the end, left the great city on foot, in the dust and the glare. Behind him, the sky was already hazy with the smoke of the burning suburbs.

A few miles out, on a quiet road, he came upon two ladies in a small carriage, who were being attacked by a pair of ruffians trying to steal their horse and their money. The brother, young and strong, threw himself into the fight, drove off the thieves with his fists, and, when the danger had passed, offered to take the reins and guide the ladies to safety. They accepted with relief and gratitude, and so it was that three strangers journeyed on toward the east together.

After many hard hours, they reached the sea, where hundreds of vessels, large and small, lay jammed together in the harbor, and thousands of frightened people crowded the beach. The brother paid a high price for places on a steamer, and the little party climbed aboard with a great sense of relief, although they could still see the smoke far inland. From the deck, the ocean looked calm, and the sun shone bright, as though no harm could ever come to that place.

Suddenly a gigantic Martian machine rose from the haze and strode into the water, and behind it came another, and a great groan of dismay rose from the fleeing vessels. Then, to everyone's astonishment, the ironclad Thunder Child came tearing through the fleet, her guns blazing, and rammed and destroyed two of the machines before the Heat-Ray had time to strike. She was destroyed herself in the end, but her sacrifice gave the steamers time to slip into the fog, and the survivors never forgot her.

In the ruins of a deserted house at Sheen, the narrator and the curate sheltered together, fearing every sound, until in the dead of night another cylinder came roaring out of the sky and struck the ground close by. The explosion threw them both across the room, the walls shook and cracked, and when the dust had cleared, they found themselves buried in rubble and half deafened by the din. The house, which had once been safe, was now a ruin beside the Martians' newest camp.

At first light, the narrator crawled across the broken floor and looked out through a small crack in the wall, and what he saw below filled him with wonder and dread. A huge pit lay open to the sky, and in it the Martians were at work, moving among half-built machines with their tentacles and speaking to one another in strange, high tones. It was the first time that any human being had been allowed to watch them at their labor.

He could see that they were scarcely more than heads, with great dark eyes and a cluster of delicate, quivering hands, and that they had no bodies to speak of, and no need of any. The narrator saw, too, that they did not eat as we do, but fed instead on the fresh blood of living creatures, which they took directly into their veins. The sight made him turn away in disgust, and for a while he lay still, breathing hard against the cold floor.

For many days, the two men were prisoners in the broken house, creeping about on hands and knees and speaking only in whispers, afraid that the Martians might hear them. They had little to eat but a few scraps of bread and little to drink, and the narrator learned how bitter hunger and fear can be. Outside, the great machines passed back and forth, their steps shaking the ground, while the men shrank back from the broken window.

As the days dragged by, the curate fell into a fever of weakness and despair, and he began to mutter, to pray aloud and to curse, until the narrator could scarcely bear it. Time and again, he begged the man to be silent, but the curate's mind had given way, and he no longer understood what he was doing. The narrator knew in his heart that sooner or later the Martians would hear him, and that nothing he could say would prevent it.

One afternoon, the curate's shouting grew so loud that it carried across the pit, and the narrator heard the dull clang of a Martian machine turning toward the house. A long, flexible arm came creeping through the hole in the wall, searching about the room, and the narrator, crouched in the dark of the kitchen, held his breath as it passed over his head. When it withdrew, the curate was gone, and the narrator knew that he had been taken.

For days afterward, the narrator stayed hidden in the dark of the scullery, listening and afraid, eating what scraps he could find, until his strength began to fade. At last, one morning, he realized that the usual sounds from the pit had stopped, and that a silence as deep as the grave had settled over the place. Cautiously, with a hammering heart, he crept toward the crack in the wall to see what had happened.

When he looked out at last, the great pit was empty, and the huge machines had vanished, and over everything lay the sun, bright and pitiless. Wherever he turned, a strange red weed, brought by the Martians from their home planet, had crept across the landscape, covering the ruins, the fields and even the very rivers with a thick red carpet. It seemed to him that the whole of England was being slowly dyed the color of blood.

He climbed out of the ruins and set off toward London, because he could think of nowhere else to go, and he walked for hours across a landscape of silent houses and dead fields. On the green slope of Putney Hill, he came upon the artilleryman he had met before, thin, dirty and strangely cheerful, who hailed him like an old friend. The two men sat down together on the grass, and the soldier began, with a hungry eagerness, to talk.

The artilleryman declared that the day of the common man was over, and that those who wished to survive must go beneath the ground and build a new world among the sewers and tunnels. He drew his plan in the dust: a great city of deep halls, with clever men and healthy women, which would one day take the planet back from the Martians. His eyes shone as he spoke, and the narrator listened with growing sympathy and then with growing doubt.

But as the hours went by, the narrator understood that his companion was a dreamer who loved to talk, and who would never lift a spade, or do any of the labor that his plan demanded. At last, with sadness and a little scorn, he shook the man's hand, wished him luck and went on his way, leaving him alone upon the hill. He knew, with a curious certainty, that he would never see the man again, and he did not look back as he walked down the long slope of the hill.

The streets of London lay silent under the pale sun, the great houses stood with their doors open and their windows dark, and the city seemed to hold its breath. Then, from somewhere across the roofs, there came a long, wailing, mournful cry, rising and falling like the howl of a lost animal, and the words were always the same: “Ulla, ulla, ulla, ulla.” It was the saddest and loneliest sound that the narrator had ever heard in all his life, and it made the silent streets seem even emptier than before.

He was so tired, so alone and so weary of hiding that he felt he no longer cared whether he lived or died, and he began to walk straight toward the sound. Across the wide, deserted grass of the park he went, with his eyes on the green hill ahead, feeling strangely calm and almost glad. If the Martians were still there, he thought, then let them finish what they had begun.

At the top of Primrose Hill, he found a gigantic machine standing motionless on its three tall legs, with its head bowed forward as if in sleep. Within its hood, tangled in the metal, lay a dead Martian, and around it the black crows and the stray dogs were feeding on what they found. The narrator stared, then laughed and wept at once, and a great weight rolled off his heart.

All across the city, he found others, dead Martians in their machines and Martians lying where they had fallen, and everywhere the silence of the grave. The cry that he had heard was the last despairing call of the final survivor, who had died only a short time before, far away, among the buildings. He sat on the grass and understood that the great invasion was over, and that the world was free.

Afterward, the learned men said that the Martians, who had no defense against the ordinary germs that fill our air, our water and our food, had been killed by the smallest and most humble creatures on Earth. Mankind, which had been shaped by the long fight with disease, had grown immune over countless ages, and its old enemies had at last turned out to be its saviors. No army, no weapon, and no cleverness could have done what these tiny germs did.

The narrator sat for a long time and wept, and as the sun rose higher, the people of London began to creep out of their cellars and attics to look at the clear blue sky and one another. The word spread from street to street, and from house to house, that the Martians were dead, and a great sound of joy rose from the city. Day by day, as the news was carried from house to house and from town to town, the old life began to come back to the stricken city.

Weak with hunger and weariness, the narrator fell ill, and he was taken in and cared for by a kind family who gave him a bed, soup and quiet. Little by little, as he mended, he heard how the terror had spread across the whole world and how it had ended at last in the same strange way. He lay back in his bed, listening, and he felt as if he had returned from the dead.

All over the world, from the great capitals to the smallest villages, people heard that the Martians had perished, and a vast wave of thanks and relief swept the globe. The trains began to run again, the shops opened their shutters, and the families that had fled returned to their homes, which were scarred but still standing. Mankind had been spared at the very edge of destruction, and the nations, which so lately had despaired, rejoiced together in a way that they had never done before.

When he was strong enough, the narrator took a train and went back to Woking, and to the house where he had once lived so quietly, and which seemed to him now like a place in a dream. The garden was a wilderness of weeds, the front gate hung off its hinges, and the whole house stood silent in the sunlight, with a coat of dust on every window. He stepped inside, and every room told of the life that had been lost.

As he stood at his study door, thinking of what he had suffered, he heard a quiet footstep in the hall behind him, and a voice that he knew spoke his name. He turned, and there, in the light of the open door, stood his wife, whom he had thought dead, and who looked at him with eyes that were full of joy. For a long moment, as the sun streamed in through the open door and the dust danced in the light, he could not speak a single word.

They stood in the doorway and held each other without a word, while the sun shone warm on their shoulders and the garden gate swung in the wind. The narrator, who had been through the end of the world and had come out the other side, felt a thankfulness deeper than any he had known. He knew then that nothing in life could ever be taken for granted again.

The great machines of the Martians were carried away and placed in the museums of the world, where crowds came to wonder at them, and scientists measured and studied every piece. From them, the men of science learned much about the bodies and minds of those who had come so close to conquering the Earth. It was said that our own inventions advanced by many years in those few months.

The invasion changed forever how people thought about their place in the universe, for it was now plain that the Earth was only one small world among countless others. Mankind could no longer believe that it was alone, or that its home was a safe and private place that no one could ever enter. A quiet humility fell upon the great nations in the months that followed, and it did them a great deal of good, though it was not always remembered.

On clear nights, the narrator liked to stand in his garden and look up at the red glow of Mars, so small and silent in the distance, and wonder what lay behind it. Perhaps the Martians would try again, with better weapons and better knowledge, or perhaps one day men themselves would build ships that could cross the dark gulf between the worlds. He could not tell, but he knew that the future would be very strange.

The people around him seemed changed, for they were gentler, quieter and more thoughtful, and they went about their lives with a new appreciation of how little it takes to destroy everything. In shops and in streets, the narrator saw strangers help one another, and it seemed to him that the great trial had left behind it something precious. The peril had been terrible, but it had also taught mankind to value its peace.

The narrator now lives a quiet life, working at his desk and walking in his garden, but sometimes, in the dead of night, he wakes in a cold sweat from a dream of the black machines. Then he turns and sees his wife sleeping peacefully beside him, and the fear slowly drains away, leaving only the quiet of the dark room. He lies there for a long while in the stillness, thinking of all that has happened, until the first gray light of morning creeps around the curtains.

He looks at the world with different eyes now, because he has seen how quickly everything can be swept away, and how little separates the quiet of a summer evening from the end of all things. The sun on the road, the scent of rain and the green of an English field, all these things have become infinitely dear to him. He has learned, at an awful price, to see how beautiful it all is.

So the narrator ends his story with a feeling of deep gratitude, not for any great victory, but for the plain and ordinary things of life that nearly slipped from his grasp. In the quiet of the evening, with the lamp lit and his wife beside him, he looks up through the window at the first star of the night. There it shines, calm and bright, and he lets it shine, knowing that for now, at least, all is well.
